introduction.content: Nearly all my paintings begin on a screen and end on canvas. There is a reason for that: I belong to the last generation, the millennials, that studied without screens, with paper and pen, and then had to make its way in a digital environment. The same doubleness runs through my working life. I divide my time between the craft of art and the design and development of software, the most ethereal of the crafts.

painting.title: Painting
painting.limits: Painting is a practice as old as humanity itself. And a painter can work a surface as much as he wants; painting’s only limits are space and time. In theory those are infinite resources, but from a human point of view they are finite: the space we can take in, and the time of one life.
painting.recontextualising: Giving time and space to an image that originally had neither (a scroll is not a physical place, and the time given to an image there is minimal) changes its meaning completely. In giving it that time, that importance, you recontextualise the image, and open up the chance of finding new meanings in it. The craft itself does the same work: a casual moment fixed in oil takes on another dimension.
painting.rule: As a general rule, the larger the work and the more time given to it, the better.

images.title: Decontextualised images
images.found: For years I found them by chance on the internet, which was already a more or less infinite visual world before generative AI arrived. Between 2019 and 2023 I began using neural networks (StyleGAN, BigBiGAN) while they still “failed” considerably. That margin of error, the so-called “loss”, produced monsters no human could have come up with. My interest in painting them comes out of that fascination. Those tools have since reached a formal competence that interests me a good deal less: because they get it right too often. AI since 2023 is boring for being predictable, in the same way a predictable conversation or a predictable book is boring. The better it gets, the worse. The so-called “AI slop” floods our daily lives with images that are all alike and have no character whatsoever.
images.accident: “No mistakes, just happy accidents”, as Bob Ross used to say. What serves an artist is the accident, the singular. The software that deforms an image until it aberrates. Failure is working material.

failure.title: Failure
failure.content: “I have done many things because I have failed at all of them. I start from failure as one of the Fine Arts.” The line is from the multifaceted Pepín Tre, and it explains fairly well why I end up in such different techniques and registers. Genius and inspiration are comfortable clichés long past their sell-by date; what actually pushes you to try something else is the last thing having failed. Success, real or perceived, is paralysing. Or so I want to believe.

project.title: juanmamoreno.com, the product
project.lead: It is built on on-chain certificates of authenticity owned by the artist, a catalogue anybody can browse, and a set of tools that automate the digital workflows that come out of his work.
project.lead2: The solution delegates implementation, along with the test and deployment pipelines, to AI agents. The flow is automated: the product owner puts requirements to the agent, and the agent implements them, runs the unit tests and the end-to-end tests, makes sure the requirements that were already there still hold, and deploys the front end and the services.

figures.requirements: requirements, each with a reason and unit and end-to-end tests that keep it alive

about.title: Where I am coming from
about.a: Ten years as a full-stack developer, two as a tech lead and two as a designer, over a background in artistic creation and design.
about.b: Working as a developer I was always the kind who cared more about defining and designing the solution than implementing it. Deciding what was worth building, and why, was what mattered most to me. That is why I usually worked close to the product owners.
about.c: Now that agents have taken over almost all of the implementation, and almost all of the problem-solving, moving toward product design is the natural progression for me.

product.title: The product, and what it is for
product.lead: Three things, in the order they were built.

one.name: Certificates of authenticity
one.body: A certificate of authenticity for every physical work, written to a public chain (Ethereum) where the artist alone holds the key. No intermediary to trust, no fees and no dependencies. The record is written inside the chain rather than linked from it, so the certificates are a thing of their own that outlives this app and even the artist.

two.name: A catalogue anybody can read
two.body: The work — physical and generative — laid out so that anyone can move through it, narrow it, generate the technical sheet as a pdf, download a certificate of authenticity as a pdf, an essay about the painting, or a list of links to where that painting turns up on the internet. 192 on-chain paintings come to some 400 static pages in English and Spanish, every one of them readable with no JavaScript at all.

three.name: A tool for the artist
three.body: The week-to-week work, automated: correcting the photograph of a canvas, cutting it to the frame, taking the glare off, setting the levels, then writing and translating the text, recording the work on the chain, and publishing the images and the video that were generated for it. All of it is built so that the human part is as small as it can be.

architecture.title: How it is put together
architecture.a: The site is static in the strict sense. Every page, in both languages, is written to disk before it is published and served as a file: there is no server rendering anything, and so no server to fall over, to patch or to pay for. The build refuses to publish itself if a page has come out wrong.
architecture.b: Behind it, a private containerised service does the rest: it prepares the photographs and the thumbnails, writes and translates the essays using language models, renders the video, runs reverse image searches, publishes to the social networks and assembles the chain transactions. What it produces goes to a document database, and the large files to a bucket.
architecture.c: The blockchain is Ethereum. Each certificate is a token whose content — title, medium, dimensions, year and a small photograph — is written inside the chain rather than pointed at from it, so nothing has to stay online for the record to be readable. The web-resolution images live in permanent decentralised storage.

diagram.caption: Who asks what of whom, and who signs.

agents.title: Readers that are not people
agents.a: The site was already made legible to machines: because every page is written to disk before it is published, the text is in the HTML and nothing has to run to read it; each work carries its structured data; and the file that governs crawlers names the language models’ own crawlers one by one and lets them in. Legible, though, is not usable: comparing ten paintings meant asking for ten pages and picking them apart.
agents.b: The whole catalogue is now published as a single file as well: title, year, medium, dimensions, whether it is available, the text in both languages, the image, both addresses of the page and the certificate token. The build writes it from the pages themselves, so it cannot contradict them, and the build refuses to publish if the file stops agreeing with what was made.
agents.c: That interface now exists: the service speaks the MCP protocol at backend.juanmamoreno.com/mcp, and an assistant that adds it once can, in the middle of a conversation, search the work by year, size, medium or availability, read one of them with its essay, and check a certificate against the chain. Three tools, all of them reading: none writes, sends, or costs money per request. It answers from the same file the site publishes, so it cannot say anything the site does not already say in public, and an essay goes out only once I have been over it.
agents.d: Prices are in neither, and will not be. That is not an oversight: every price is quoted by the artist for the particular work, and an agent that answered with a figure would end the conversation the catalogue exists to begin.

rot.title: Keeping control
rot.intro: In my view, losing control of the requirements, of whether they still hold, and of how they were implemented is the main risk we take on when working with agents. So the work has been channelled along these lines:
rot.a: REQUIREMENTS DOCUMENT: a requirements document is a claim about the present. Those claims are checked by naming the thing that proves them. A script reads the file before every deploy and refuses the build if a number is used twice, if an entry has no test, if a test names a file that has been deleted, or if it quotes a test that has been renamed.
rot.b: It also reports, of course, the requirements whose only proof is the text itself — since this is a one-person project, any Agile task-management tool has been done without entirely.
rot.c: GUIDANCE DOCUMENT: a guidance document for language models that sets limits and states a preference about how to work. The idea is not to delegate sensitive decisions one hundred per cent — those about architecture, development practice or writing tests, for instance.
